utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case IT-95-9-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, Stevan Todorovic, Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the appearances starting with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Nancy Paterson representing the Office of the Prosecutor. With me today is Susan Lamb, another legal advisor with the Office of the Prosecutor and Andrew Powell the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Deyan Brashich for the Todorovic Defence. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Igor Pantelic on behalf of Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic for Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Aleksander Lazarevic, Defence counsel for Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In this motion, the accused, Stevan Todorovic, seeks an order from the Chamber for the Peace Stabilisation Force SFOR or other military and security forces operating in Bosnia and Herzegovina to furnish certain information and documents in connection with an ongoing evidentiary hearing. SFOR was invited to send a representative to this hearing and to make written submissions. SFOR has made written submissions. It indicated that it would not be represented at the hearing. I should say that the Chamber is in receipt of written submissions and arguments from the Defendant and the Office of the Prosecutor. For this reason, the Chamber, while not wishing to curtail submissions from the parties, indicates that it does not expect them to be very long. We begin with Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. The way that I see us at this juncture is that we have possibly a pragmatic solution to the impasse that we find ourselves in at this present time. Perhaps the Court would wish to inquire of the Prosecutor whether or not there is any evidence that she may wish to adduce which would contradict the testimony so far adduced before this Chamber. If there is no such testimony or proof, then I submit that the Court could find that a prima facie case has been established and, if my reading of the law is correct, then this Court could order the return of Mr. Todorovic to Yugoslavia which would avoid a confrontation with SFOR and resolve the problem. Of course, this does not resolve the problem which has been raised by SFOR as to this Court's jurisdiction. However, being a pragmatist, I would urge the Court to follow the suggestion that I have respectfully made and inquire of the Prosecutor of her case in opposition. On the other hand, if that is not followed, then I will be very brief and terse. I believe that the Republic of Croatia case, the Appeals Chamber has made it very clear that this Tribunal can request of sovereign states the information that I seek. That is why this morning I have filed that such a request be directed to the United States of America because I believe it was -- the United States of America forces that were in charge of the Tuzla air force base. I have a second submission under the teachings of the Republic of Croatia decision and that is for a subpoena duces tecum to be directed to the Commanding General of SFOR which would specify the items and documents and informations that I seek and a further subpoena ad testificandum directed to the General, and I'm using it phonetically, first name unknown -- Eric, thank you, Mr. Pantelic -- Chizeki [phoen] who was the Commanding General at Tuzla air force base in September of 1998 and then John Doe's one through ten that I have identified in the filing this morning. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Paterson.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll keep in mind your admonition to be short. I think it's important that we all understand what the issues are that we're discussing here today. And toward that end I'd like to go back to some statements made by three of Your Honours in previous proceedings before this Court. On the 4th of March, 1999, when we held oral argument, Judge Bennouna pointed out that there were two issues before the Court in relation to Mr. Brashich's motions. The first was to see whether there was any kind of collusion between the Office of the Prosecutor or any personnel of the Tribunal and any kind of unlawful activity. And as Judge Bennouna stated, and I'm quoting from the transcript, "You," referring to Mr. Brashich, "told us in your written document that the answer was no. And I assume that you still insist that negative answer." Meaning that Mr. Brashich has already conceded that he has absolutely no evidence that the Office of the Prosecutor was involved in any way in any unlawful arrest of Mr. Todorovic. In addition, Judge Bennouna went on to point out, "The second issue is whether or not the rights of Mr. Todorovic that are granted to him under the International Covenant on Human Rights or the European Human Rights Convention, whether any of those rights were violated." And Judge Bennouna pointed out that those rights have to do with procedural issues whether Mr. Todorovic was arrested pursuant to a lawful arrest warrant. Then additionally during that hearing, Judge Robinson also stated that, "If an evidentiary hearing was granted," put the question, "wouldn't the evidentiary hearing, if granted, assist in showing whether there was any connection between the OTP and the alleged abduction." Again, the issue becomes whether the OTP was involved in any unlawful activity. Now, I would point out that if you look at the motion filed by Mr. Brashich, the material that he is requesting from SFOR are things such as the attendance of the person who flew the helicopter, the attendance of the person who placed the defendant under arrest, and copies of audio and videotapes made at Tuzla air base at the time of the arrest. And the original SFOR rearrest and post-arrest operation report. It's the position of the Office of the Prosecutor that none of that evidence, even if it were made available to the defendant, would in any way show any evidence whatsoever that the Office of the Prosecutor was involved in any illegal activity. If Mr. Brashich wants to allege that the Defendant was unlawfully arrested, then that issue must be taken up with the courts of Serbia. That is not an issue before this Court. As all three of Your Honours have stated, the issue is whether the OTP was involved in any way and whether the Defendant was arrested pursuant to a lawful arrest warrant. In response to Mr. Brashich's question, if we are going to continue the hearing that we started back in November, yes, the Office of the Prosecutor would like the opportunity to present some evidence. That evidence would be a certified copy of the lawful arrest warrant and a copy of the arrest report prepared by the investigator who effected the arrest. We believe that those two pieces of evidence, along with all the other submissions by the Office of the Prosecutor, will show that there was no unlawful activity on the part of the Office of the Prosecutor. Whether or not this Court has the right to issue subpoenas or orders to SFOR, it's our contention that it is not the issue before the Court today. The issue is whether any of the information Mr. Brashich is seeking could in any way further the two questions: the involvement of the Office of the Prosecutor and the lawfulness of the arrest warrant. It's our contention that none of the information he was seeking would in any way provide that information, and unless he can provide an offer of proof to the contrary, we believe that that's quite clear and we would respectfully request that this Court refer to Rule 54 bis, specifically the section which allows the Trial Chamber to reject the application for a motion and order if the documents or information sought are not relevant to any matter in issue in the proceedings before them. It's our contention that the documents and the information that Mr. Brashich is seeking are not relevant to the issue of OTP involvement and the lawfulness of the arrest warrant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson, I'm wondering whether you have correctly perceived what the application is that Mr. Brashich makes. He started off on what in common law countries is called a fishing expedition, and which apparently is allowed in the United States but which is not allowed here. The Appeals Chamber has already had to deal with that. He then sought to identify particular documents and the video, which he wanted, and also particular witnesses to attend. Now, his concession that he had no evidence was correct. He has no evidence. What he is doing, as I understand him, is seeking evidence, which may well demonstrate some part that the OTP has had to play in this arrest. Now, he may be right, he may be wrong, but having given evidence that there was a representative of the OTP there at the time when he arrived, he says, and he may or may not be right, that that demonstrates a sufficient basis upon which he seeks these reports. Now, the Trial Chamber made an order first of all against the Prosecution to provide reports that it had received from the SFOR people. The Prosecution, after some delay, said it had no reports. It did not, I hasten to add, and never has had any -- you might perhaps enlighten us as to whether it ever did have any reports -- and it would have been sufficient if the OTP had produced them. But the OTP, either not having them or having got rid of them, is unable to comply with the order that was made, so he then goes back one stage and seeks an order against SFOR or the components of SFOR. Now, you can't say because he hasn't yet got any evidence the case must fail. What he is still trying to do is to get some evidence. And as I say, he may or he may not be successful. I should also add that his submissions, very detailed submissions he's made, seems to go beyond the premise that you are proceeding on, that he is seeking to produce evidence against the OTP. As I understand his further submissions, he is seeking to argue that it doesn't matter whether the OTP was involved or not. He wanted to go beyond what might be called the domestic decisions on the point and to say that international law is so pure that if there's any problem at any stage in the line of behaviour that leads to the arrest, then somehow he has to be set free. Now, again he may be right or he may be wrong. It's a surprising submission, but it's not restricted to the one that you suggested, that he was seeking only to prove that the OTP was involved. Now, I think you have to face up to that. I, for myself, would be very interested to know whether the OTP ever did have any reports from SFOR in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will state today, as I have stated on several occasions, the OTP had absolutely no involvement in the arrest of Stevan Todorovic and the OTP never possessed any documents related to the arrest of Stevan Todorovic other than the single document that we have already disclosed to the Defence, that being a brief, one-page report written by the investigator who made the arrest at Tuzla air base on the date in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We have not yet seen the whole of that document, of course. We've only seen --

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: That is the whole document, Your Honour. There is nothing else besides that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What, with all the spaces in it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: That is the style that the person who wrote the report wrote it in. What I'd suggest is that perhaps we could continue the hearing that we started in November, perhaps call the investigator. We're more than willing to have him come and give testimony. Let him be questioned, let him explain exactly what he did, what he knew, what he did not know, and at that point in time perhaps the Court would be in a better position to know if any of the documents that Mr. Brashich is seeking are truly relevant. Because I can give you an offer of proof that the investigator will come and state, as I have, unequivocally he knew nothing in advance about the arrest of Mr. Todorovic, the Office of the Prosecutor was not involved in any way in his arrest, and he was there as a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor simply to take the defendant into custody, to advise him of his rights, to provide him with a copy of the indictment and the arrest warrant. The Office of the Prosecutor has an investigator present at every single arrest that is made in Bosnia or Croatia in relation to the people indicted by the Tribunal. We have investigators present in other countries where arrests are made. If you are going to say that the mere fact that an investigator was present to effect the arrest opens the door to the right of any Defence counsel to seek these documents from SFOR, then I contend we are opening quite a Pandora's box that will be very difficult to close. You cannot say that the Office of the Prosecutor doesn't have a right to send an investigator to effect the arrest. The simple fact that they're there effecting the arrest doesn't then give rise to a right to seek documents and information from SFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to debate that with you, because I've stated what Mr. Brashich is claiming, and as I've said, he may be right or he may be wrong. But you still have not, if I may say so, faced up to his further arguments that it doesn't matter whether the OTP was involved or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, respectfully, Your Honour, I believe that we have discussed that several times in our various submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Only by saying from the bar table that the OTP had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I believe in our submissions to the original request for the evidentiary hearing, we argued that he had no right to the challenge that he was putting forth against just the general unlawfulness of his arrest. We've argued that in the appeal, we've argued that in several submissions. Our point from day one has been -- and I believe Judge Bennouna himself stated this in one of the proceedings -- that the issue is whether the OTP was involved. Whether or not SFOR might have been involved or some private citizens who might have kidnapped Mr. Todorovic were involved is not an issue that this Tribunal can exercise jurisdiction over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think I have said exactly the same thing as Judge Bennouna myself. That's my belief. But that's not the case that is being made, and we have to consider the case that is being made.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: The case -- to me, my reading of Mr. Brashich's motion is that's exactly what he's asking for, for this Court to go beyond the consideration of the involvement of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: To consider his general arrest scenario. And it's our contention that this Tribunal does not have jurisdiction over that issue, that even if he can make such a case, that issue is before the courts of Serbia, not before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, then come back a stage. Let's leave his further claim to one side. What do you say to his claim that he should be entitled to these documents, having identified them, in order to demonstrate that the OTP was involved? Now, all you have said so far to that is, from the bar table, "We were not involved." That, if I may say so, is hardly an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as an officer of the Court, I believe it is a legitimate statement to make, and I believe if Mr. Brondum comes and is put under oath, he will make a similar statement to that effect, that the OTP was not involved. Now, you characterise this as a fishing expedition, and frankly, we feel that is an appropriate characterisation. If Mr. Brashich cannot put forward any further offer of proof that there is reason to believe that the Office of the Prosecutor was in fact involved in any illegal activity, then it's our contention that this is nothing more than a fishing expedition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But we have already made an order against the OTP to produce these documents and this video, and you unsuccessfully appealed against it. Now, for myself, I haven't changed my mind. From my point of view, the material that was placed before us the last time justified us in making those orders against the OTP. And, as I have said, you have unsuccessfully appealed against that order. If those documents should have been made available from the OTP and the OTP hasn't got it, what do you say to the various countries who comprise SFOR being ordered to produce the same documents and video? You can't really continue to argue that they're irrelevant if we've already determined that they are matters which should be produced.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: But other than the fact that Mr. Todorovic, in his testimony here, has alleged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, no. Please. You have said that all along, and we have not accepted it. And you have to now face up to the fact we have said that those documents and that videotape should be produced by the OTP and you have lost an appeal against that order. So you have to face up to that being a justifiable order that they be produced. You say you haven't got them and you now say that you've never had them. So Mr. Brashich moves on one step back and he asks for SFOR, or the Generals Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or somebody -- I would have thought it would be the countries comprising SFOR -- to have to produce the matters which we say should be produced upon the material already before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, Your Honour, if I can put a couple of questions to you, it may help me in my argument. Are you stating that you believe that Mr. Brashich has presented sufficient evidence that this Court is of the opinion that there may in fact be evidence of OTP involvement in the arrest of Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, we haven't, and I wish you would listen to what I have said. We have followed a decision of the Appeals Chamber which says that they don't have to show that it will produce it, but that it is on the cards or that there is a reasonable possibility that it will produce. That's all. And on that basis they are entitled to have the material produced. And once again, I hope for the last time, you appealed against that and lost. Now, that is something which we have said should be produced by whoever has them. Now, you've said that you haven't got them, and he now says SFOR should produce them, or at least the Generals or somebody who is representing them. Now, what do you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: So am I to understand, then, that if, in every single case a defendant is arrested --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. Look, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: -- and brought before the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, look. I think I'm entitled to say you are not entitled to keep arguing that point. You tried it last time and you failed. We have made a decision that on the material -- which was not just that -- but on the material that was presented, we made an order that those documents and that video be produced. And you haven't been able to do it, so he now seeks it from those people who do have it. Now, what do you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: In relation to that specific issue, Your Honour, I am not a representative of SFOR. I'm not authorised to speak on behalf of SFOR. I can only speak on behalf of the OTP. The OTP has applied with all your orders. The OTP has turned over every document we've ever had in our possession related to the arrest of Mr. Todorovic. As to whether or not you have a right to order SFOR to turn over documents, we contend that that is not a right that you have. But as to whether or not an argument should be made, that argument needs to be made by SFOR. I cannot make that argument on their behalf. They have filed their written submissions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You have nothing further to say beyond what they've said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Because they haven't faced up to that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: We basically stand in agreement with the submission of SFOR, which we think for the most part reflects all of our previous submissions and all of our arguments, but I cannot speak on behalf of SFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask Mr. Brashich a question. Mr. Brashich, perhaps you could help us, because you tell us, in your Defence reply to the submission made by SFOR, which is a document dated 9th of July, and you list several things on pages 7 and 8, page 9. You remind us of the Tadic jurisprudence in this Tribunal. You say individuals can now invoke as defence violations of state sovereignty [In English] and pass upon such claim. [Interpretation] And then you develop this as follows: You tell us [In English] to plead the violation of the sovereignty of the state as a defence is not the exclusive right of states, but that individuals do, in fact and in law, have standing to challenge violations of international law and invoke violations of sovereignty as a defence. [Interpretation] And then you once again quote the Appeals Chamber. Now, if I understand your position well, you, in point of fact, tell us that the accused,Todorovic, is entitled to refer in his defence to the violation of sovereignty of a state, which in this case is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And that this violation, if it did indeed take place, that, to begin with, one can use that in his defence. And then you say there is then a problem. If one considers that there has been a violation of the sovereignty, then the accused has the right to go back to what you call "country of refuge; not his own country, but the country of refuge, that country where he was unlawfully arrested. In the document which was submitted by SFOR, the Peace Stabilisation Force, and the paper that was written by its legal advisor also dated 9th of July, he says as follows: "They tell us that whatever the form in which Mr. Todorovic was arrested, and even if he was arrested by violating the laws of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and therefore this might constitute a violation of the sovereignty of that state, but this cannot result in his release, that is, it cannot result in his return to this country of refuge." [As interpreted] And do I now understand properly what is then the procedure which does not end up in any results since the accused is here, he is present, and I leave aside the debate which took place between Judge Hunt and the Prosecutor regarding the possible responsibility of OTP. I am talking about the violation of sovereignty. Because what are you telling us, what you are referring to is the violation of sovereignty which could be a means, a tool of the Defence, and that could be the problem. Now, you tell us, the SFOR, even if he was unlawfully arrested, the SFOR tells us the result of this should not be his release because whatever the case, this person needs to be arrested wherever he happens to be, by virtue of the indictment, which is a valid act and in the light of the Statute of the Tribunal and its Articles, it is therefore binding on all the states, so it's what kind of -- so what is the action that you can take which will not result in anything because it is not going to result in the release of Mr. Todorovic? Now, I should like to hear what you have to tell us about this, because you have always maintained that it was evident that if somebody has been unlawfully arrested, then this sole remedy to this is the release of such a person. But then it could result in some absurd result because someone takes them to the country of refuge, and then the country of refuge is requested to send him by the same plane, by the same flight. This is not only in theory; this is also in practice. Because this -- is an indictment against this person which is valid, and he therefore needs to be delivered by whatever standard he may happen to be in. Now he is in The Hague. Now you tell us you take him back to Belgrade, and then you request Belgrade to deliver him back immediately. Would you please try to clarify this point because we should indeed like to know what you think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: The way I read the precedent in international law is that we start with the Eichman case, and we have an illegal abduction which is made legal by the failure of the state in which the abduction takes place to protest. That's the early '60s. International law has evolved and now I believe the proper view is that an illegal abduction ousts the Court of jurisdiction. We have a situation where we have a violation of state sovereignty, which my client has a vote, and which the Appeals Chamber has said is a defence that can be invoked by a defendant before this Tribunal. The practical result, Your Honour, you are quite correct, would be a return not to freedom, not liberation, but a return to the jurisdiction of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and a request, a proper request by the OTP for extradition of Mr. Todorovic to this Court, to this Tribunal, for further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I will stop you now, Mr. Brashich. The term "extradition" is not in order here because this is a technical and a legal term, and it is not used in the international jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I misspoke. For his return to the Tribunal for further proceedings pursuant to the indictment. As I have pointed out in my recent submission, to do otherwise or to follow SFOR's argument, which I believe is flawed, that this is pointless, either: One, he will be returned immediately; or two, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia will not honour its commitment made in the Dayton Accord and the Paris Peace Treaty because it has not done so which places this Tribunal in a very difficult position of having to pass upon the politics of a sovereign state. Therefore, where you return him to follow through on the proper procedure is immaterial, if it is Cuba, North Korea, Iraq, as I have pointed out, or the Netherlands. That is something, I believe, outside the scope that this Court may -- "scope" is an improper word -- beyond the interests of the Tribunal and has to be dealt in a political forum just as any request to a state for information in order to compel the receipt of such information is dealt not in the level of the Court, but at the level of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brashich, let us try to be professional, because this is not a political institution, this is the International Tribunal. You quote a number of precedents. Now, how do they concern the violation of sovereignty of a state by another state?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a question of a violation of sovereignty of a state by an international organisation because the problem that you raise here is the judgement here, it is the judgement of an International Tribunal taken on the basis of Chapter VII. You know very well that when one is within the context of Chapter VII, then the reservation of paragraph 2 in Chapter VII of the Charter which protects the domain which is reserved to the national jurisdiction of the states, that is domestic jurisdiction, that does not really, cannot play a role here. It cannot be raised because in Chapter VII, and that is quite clear, and even in paragraph 2 of Chapter VII of the Charter. So you speak about the domestic jurisdiction of the state before the Tribunal and that is the national competence of the Tribunal because this Tribunal operates on the basis of Chapter VII. Now, the question which arises here, that is which you put before us and about which our Chamber will rule in due time is that the Peace Stabilisation Force, the SFOR, which is an international organisation set up by the Security Council, that the SFOR exceeded its own competencies. That is the problem that you put before us, and I wish to conclude on this point. The mandate, the terms of reference of SFOR to arrest individuals, that do support the Tribunal is limited to the territory of the former Yugoslavia, that is Bosnia, and it transpires here that the operation took place elsewhere or it is alleged that it began elsewhere, even though it was effected in Bosnia and you, therefore, tell us that this international organisation which depends on NATO, but which was set up by the Security Council, has received a mandate by the Security Council on the basis of Chapter VII and it has exceeded the competencies which were laid down for it by the Security Council in its resolution. Is that what you are telling us? I should like to hear it from you. Is that what you are telling -- is that how -- that is how I understand things but I should like to hear how you understand things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: The Court is totally correct that all of the precedent that I have cited deal with national jurisdiction. I am unaware of an international body being involved in a kidnapping or having been brought to task for being involved in a kidnapping so I do not have a precedent to cite to the Court. I believe that Your Honour is totally correct that Article 7 which established this Tribunal also established IFOR, and then SFOR, on the territory of Bosnia. I'm going a step further, Your Honour. I'm saying that there is a vertical relationship rather than a horizontal relationship, as the Republic of Croatia suggests, between SFOR and this Tribunal. I am further suggesting, Your Honour, that participation in an abduction and seizure of a person on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, if proven, would oust this Court of jurisdiction, respectfully. And I'm going further, Your Honour, and stating that it just, at least in my point of view, cannot be a situation where an international body is not responsible to someone for any act which might be deemed illegal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Brashich. To conclude this, you tell us, and I'm reading from the transcript now, [In English] "... and seizure of a person on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." [Interpretation] Are you questioning SFOR for having taken place in this "unlawful seizure" in inverted commas, or are you questioning the Tribunal by means of the OTP? What is it that you bring into question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, primarily, but as Judge Hunt pointed out, I am seeking information which I have not received and which the OTP has not been forthcoming with that there may be some involvement on the OTP. As you recall, in the situation where we had the luring across the bridge, the OTP specifically admitted that it was a joint operation. I do not recall the citation, Your Honour -- Dokmanovic case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see, Dokmanovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: It seems odd, as Judge Hunt just pointed out, when I made a request and this Court made an order, rather than just saying, "Here is a report. That's all we have." We have a stonewalling, and we have an appeal. Then, after the appeal is lost, I receive not the original of the arrest report, a redone, remade, presently manufactured report, because the original is somehow lost in the OTP's office in Sarajevo. Is there any other points, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Brashich. If I understand you well, you tell us that you do not exclude possible complicity between the OTP in this operation of illegal abduction; is that what you mean? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, you will be able to reply briefly if you wish to the submissions from the Prosecutor, but before you do that, I just wanted to clarify something with Ms. Paterson. Ms. Paterson, to Judge Hunt, you said that you could not speak on behalf of SFOR, but my understanding is that you are not asked, you are not being asked to speak on behalf of SFOR, you are being asked as the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor to make submissions on the legal issue, and that legal issue is whether the Chamber has the competence to issue an order to SFOR. I understand you, however, to be saying that you adopt in that regard the submissions made by SFOR; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe what I said was that we have addressed that issue several times in the past in our written submissions so I don't want to repeat myself again. It's our position that this Court does not have the right to issue such an order to SFOR. While we do not adopt the statement of SFOR, I simply point out that it is basically in line with the arguments that the OTP has made, that we are essentially making the same arguments. We had no opportunity to have any input into the submission by SFOR so I don't want to claim any connection to it in that regard. Our position is, and has been all along, that there is no basis in international law for the request that Mr. Brashich is making, that the Tribunal has limited jurisdiction when it comes to these issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Paterson, to help us, you need to answer fully the question that Judge Robinson asked. My colleague, Judge Robinson, asked you a question and that is a very important question. Does the Tribunal have the possibility to -- can the Tribunal order SFOR to produce that document, because so far, we have only been asking for the document, but have not ordered it yet. I am not raising that question of the subpoena, which is a different matter and which, as you know, has to do with another problem and that problem was, in part, resolved by the Tribunal jurisprudence in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON'S QUESTION WAS
utterances.text: What is your position about this? We know that the Tribunal can issue orders to the state on the basis of Article 29. The question that I ask you, if we can order, issue an order to a particular state, why cannot we order to a certain number of states which operate through an international organisation? Now, the question is as follows: Would it be enough to hide behind an international organisation in order to avoid, to evade the orders of the International Tribunal, is that it? And we should like to hear what you think about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position is that on the basis of the facts before this Chamber, the specific facts of the arrest of Mr. Todorovic, the information that Mr. Brashich has provided, the information that we have provided, it's our position and on the basis of these facts that it is not appropriate and not within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal to order SFOR to comply. We are not stating that there are not potential circumstances under which that would be appropriate. We acknowledge the rights under the Blaskic decision, and the right to issue requests to states to provide documents. We acknowledge that but what we are saying is that this is a different factual situation, and based on the facts in this particular case, we do not think that the Tribunal has the right to order SFOR. That is not because the OTP is attempting to hide behind any international organisation, it is, as we have argued all along, based on the facts of this case. It's our point that the only issue that is before this Tribunal is whether the OTP was involved in some illegality, and the arguments that Mr. Brashich go to extradition issues, state sovereignty issues and issues of that nature that are not within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Paterson. Do you wish to reply? If so, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Not really, Your Honour. The only thing which I would say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Blaskic decision is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you. I've made the written submissions and the arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thank the parties for the submissions that have been made. The Chamber will consider this matter and give a decision as soon as possible. The hearing is adjourned.
